html:
The big picture

A robot senses, processes and actuates; this lecture follows the sensing side into the computer and back out as a plan. Every measurement has an error: random errors scatter the readings (reduce them by averaging), systematic errors shift them (correct them by calibration), and the uncertainty states how far the result can be trusted. To be processed, an analog signal is sampled (discrete in time) and quantised (discrete in amplitude), giving a digital signal of binary numbers — and the sampling theorem says how fast you must sample. Signals are built from sinusoids; the Fourier transform shows that frequency content, and filters (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch) keep the frequencies you want. The last part is path planning: describe the world as a graph — a visibility graph (shortest paths, close to obstacles) or a Voronoi graph (maximum clearance) — and search it for the shortest path.

Automation system

ENVIRONMENT → SENSE → PROCESS → ACTUATE → back to the environment.

Measurement

  • The objective of a measurement is to determine the value of the measurand.
  • Measurand — the particular quantity subjected to measurement (e.g. the temperature of the room, the distance to an object).
  • Measurement — a set of operations carried out to determine the value of the measurand.
  • Example: the temperature of the room is 24.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}.

Measurement errors and uncertainty

  • Measurements have imperfections that give rise to an error:
\text{Error} = \text{measured value} - \text{true value}
  • True value — the value attributed to a particular quantity and accepted, sometimes by convention, as having an uncertainty appropriate for a given purpose.

  • Random error:

    • arises from unpredictable variations of influence quantities;
    • can be reduced by increasing the number of measurements.

  • Systematic error:

    • arises from imperfections in the measurement process and instruments (bias, nonlinearity, etc.);
    • cannot be eliminated fully but can often be corrected.

  • Uncertainty: a parameter associated with the result of a measurement that characterises the dispersion of the values that could reasonably be attributed to the measurand.

    • Example: the temperature of the room is 24\,^\circ\mathrm{C} (\pm 0.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}).

True value — fit for purpose: a lab balance to measure 3 g of sodium chloride (NaCl) vs. a spoon for measuring 3 g of salt in the kitchen. Both are "right" for their purpose.

Rows: low bias / high bias. Columns: low variance / high variance. Low bias = the shots centre on the bullseye; low variance = they cluster tightly.

Intuition

Bias is the systematic error — the whole cloud of shots is shifted; variance is the random error — the cloud is spread. The common words: accuracy = close to the true value (low bias), precision = close to each other (low variance). Bottom-left on the target is the treacherous one: very precise, consistently wrong. Averaging more readings shrinks the spread but never moves the cloud back to the centre.

Common mistake

"If I average enough readings, the error goes away." Averaging reduces only the random part. A thermometer that reads 1\,^\circ\mathrm{C} too high reads 1\,^\circ\mathrm{C} too high on average too. Systematic errors need calibration against a reference — a known weight, a known distance, an ice bath.

Unclear (slide 7)

Recomputing from the table: mean = 24.23 ✓, but the standard deviation is about 0.25 (sample standard deviation; 0.24 population), not 0.08. Even without the outlier 23.61 it is about 0.13. The mean is right; the printed spread is too small.

Measurement example — weight over ten days

Day12345678910
Weight70.569.371.269.471.571.269.76768.570.1

Mean = 69.8, standard deviation = 1.4 (scatter plot of the ten values; the target shows a wide spread around the centre).

Worked example — mean and standard deviation of the weight data
  1. Mean: \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i = \frac{698.4}{10} = 69.84.
  2. Deviations, squared, summed: \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \approx 17.32.
  3. Sample standard deviation: s = \sqrt{\frac{17.32}{n - 1}} = \sqrt{1.924} \approx 1.39 — matches the slide's 1.4.
  4. Read it: a single day's reading typically lies about 1.4 kg from the mean. The mean of the ten is much more certain: its standard error is s/\sqrt{n} \approx 0.44\,\mathrm{kg} — that's "random errors shrink with more measurements" in numbers.
Why does averaging n readings shrink the random error by \sqrt{n}, not by n?

Random errors are equally likely to be positive or negative, so in a sum they partly cancel. The sum of n independent errors with spread \sigma has spread \sqrt{n}\,\sigma (variances add, standard deviations don't); dividing by n for the mean leaves \sigma/\sqrt{n}. So four times as many readings only halves the error — precision gets expensive quickly.

Analog-to-digital conversion

ANALOG → SENSING SYSTEM → DIGITAL.

A small introduction to computers — the transistor

  • A transistor is a switch: a control voltage V_{\mathrm{CONTROL}} decides whether current I_{\mathrm{DRAIN}} flows between V_1 and V_2.
  • Two states: HIGH / TRUE / ON / 1 and LOW / FALSE / OFF / 0.

Boolean logic

ABANDORXORNANDNORXNOR
00000111
10011100
01011100
11110001
Intuition

AND = "both", OR = "at least one", XOR = "exactly one" (the inputs differ). The N-versions are the same gates followed by NOT — the small circle on the gate symbol. XNOR is 1 exactly when the inputs are equal, which makes it a one-bit comparator.

Decimal number system

5207 is a base-10 number; each digit has 10 possible values, 0, \dots, 9:

5207 = 5 \times 10^3 + 2 \times 10^2 + 0 \times 10^1 + 7 \times 10^0 = 5 \times 1000 + 2 \times 100 + 0 \times 10 + 7 \times 1
Unclear (slide 12)

The last term is printed as 7 \times 10^1; it must be 7 \times 10^0 (= 7 \times 1, as the line below it correctly says).

Binary number system

Base 2 — each bit has 2 possible values, 0 and 1:

11011101_2 = 1\cdot 2^7 + 1\cdot 2^6 + 0\cdot 2^5 + 1\cdot 2^4 + 1\cdot 2^3 + 1\cdot 2^2 + 0\cdot 2^1 + 1\cdot 2^0 = 128 + 64 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 221_{10}
Symbols
  • The subscript gives the base: 11011101_2 is written in base 2 (binary), 221_{10} in base 10 (decimal)
  • Each bit is multiplied by 2 to the power of its position, counting from 0 at the rightmost bit

"There are 10 types of people in the world … those who understand binary and those who don't."

Exercise: what is 110101_2 in base 10?

Worked example — 110101_2 in base 10
  1. Label the places from the right, starting at 2^0: the bits are 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1 for 2^5, 2^4, 2^3, 2^2, 2^1, 2^0.
  2. Keep the places with a 1: 32 + 16 + 4 + 1.
  3. Add: 53_{10}.
  4. Check backwards by repeated halving: 53 \to remainder 1, 26 \to 0, 13 \to 1, 6 \to 0, 3 \to 1, 1 \to 1; read bottom-up: 110101 ✓.

Signal processing

  • A signal is a set of information or data.
  • Signals can be scalar or vector (temperature, pressure, position, velocity).
  • Signals can be analog or digital (or discrete).

(The slides spell "discrete" as "discreet" throughout.)

Analog / continuous signals

  • A finite, real-valued, smooth function s(t) of a variable t, which usually represents time.
  • Both s and t in s(t) are continuous.

Sampling — discrete in time

Sampling is the process of acquiring information at periodic intervals: the continuous S(t) is read every T seconds, giving samples S_i.

A continuous signal S(t) sampled at intervals T (sample points S_i at 0, 1, \dots, 13).

Discrete signals

  • A discrete-time signal is a bounded, continuous-valued sequence s[n]. Alternatively, it may be viewed as a continuous-valued function of a discrete index n.
  • We often refer to the index n as time, since discrete-time signals are frequently obtained by sampling a continuous-time signal.

Discrete vs. digital

  • We work with digital signals but develop the theory mainly around discrete-time signals.
  • Digital computers deal with digital signals rather than discrete-time signals.
  • A digital signal is a sequence s[n] that can only take a finite set of values.
  • Digital signals are discrete-time signals obtained after quantisation.
  • Digital signals too are usually obtained by measuring real-world phenomena. However, unlike the accepted norm for analog signals, digital signals may take complex values.

Quantisation

Quantisation is the process of discretising the amplitude of the signal.

A continuous signal (blue), its samples (orange) and the quantised output (green), each rounded to one of 16 levels with 4-bit codes 0000–1111.

Intuition — the two steps of A/D conversion
timeamplitude
analogcontinuouscontinuous
discrete-time (sampled)discretecontinuous
digital (sampled + quantised)discretediscrete

Sampling decides when you look; quantisation decides how finely you can write down what you saw. An n-bit converter has 2^n levels, so its resolution is about \frac{\text{range}}{2^n}: a 10-bit ADC over 0–5 V distinguishes steps of about 5/1024 \approx 4.9\,\mathrm{mV}. Quantisation always adds an error of up to half a step.

Common signals

  • DC (constant) signal: takes a constant value, e.g. s(t) = 5. It typically represents any constant offset from 0 in real-world signals.
  • Unit step (Heaviside function): literally a step — value 0 until time 0, where it abruptly switches to 1. It represents events that change state, e.g. switching on a system or another signal.
  • Sinusoid — the most important signal in all of signal processing:
s(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \phi), \qquad \omega = 2\pi f

with A the amplitude, \omega the angular frequency, f the frequency and \phi the phase. A sine wave is completely described by its amplitude, frequency and phase.

Symbols
  • s(t) — the signal's value at time t; t — time (s)
  • A — amplitude: the peak value (in the signal's unit, e.g. V)
  • \omega — angular frequency (rad/s); f — frequency: cycles per second (Hz)
  • \phi — phase (rad): shifts the wave in time; at t = 0 the wave is at angle \phi of its cycle
Connection

The unit step is exactly the "reference jumps to a new value" input used to judge controllers in 6 Dynamics & Control — the step responses there are a system's answer to u(t).

Composite signals

  • A composite signal is a sum of many simple sinusoids with different frequencies, amplitudes and phases.
  • It can be periodic or non-periodic.
  • A periodic composite signal can be decomposed into simple sine waves with discrete frequencies that are integer multiples (1, 2, 3, … times the base frequency).
  • A non-periodic composite signal decomposes into infinitely many sine waves with continuous (real-valued) frequencies.

Sampling theorem

  • The sample rate must be at least twice the highest frequency component of the signal to capture all information.
  • In practice, because of the finite time available, a sample rate somewhat higher than this is necessary.
Why twice the highest frequency — and what goes wrong below it?

To pin down a sinusoid you need at least something like a sample on each "up" and each "down" half of every cycle — two samples per period. Sample slower and a fast sinusoid produces exactly the same samples as a slower one: it is aliased onto a false, lower frequency, and nothing after the converter can tell them apart. Example: a 30 Hz signal sampled at 40 Hz advances \frac{30}{40} = 0.75 of a cycle per sample, which looks identical to going back 0.25 of a cycle — a 10 Hz signal (\lvert 30 - 40 \rvert). That's the "wagon wheel turning backwards" effect in films. Strictly, the rate must be greater than twice f_{\max} (exactly twice can land every sample on a zero crossing), and real systems put an analog anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the converter so no frequency above half the sample rate gets in.

Worked example — choosing a sample rate
  1. Signal: a vibration sensor on a robot joint whose relevant content goes up to f_{\max} = 200\,\mathrm{Hz}.
  2. Theorem: sample at more than 2 \cdot 200 = 400\,\mathrm{Hz}.
  3. Practice: choose clearly more — e.g. 1\,\mathrm{kHz} — and low-pass filter the analog signal below 500\,\mathrm{Hz} (half the sample rate) so higher-frequency noise can't alias down into the band you care about.

Filtering

  • In signal processing, a filter is a device or process that removes some unwanted components or features from a signal.
  • Filtering is a class of signal processing whose defining feature is the complete or partial suppression of some aspect of the signal.
  • Most often, this means removing some frequencies or frequency bands.
  • Filtering is the process of enhancing desired features of a signal or suppressing unwanted features.
  • Picture on the slide: a noisy signal in time → a low-pass frequency response → the smooth signal in time.

Fourier transform

The Fourier transform turns a function of time, x(t), into a function of frequency, X(\omega):

F(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)\,e^{-i\omega t}\,dt, \qquad f(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} F(\omega)\,e^{i\omega t}\,d\omega
Symbols
  • f(t) — the signal in the time domain (the text above calls it x(t)); t — time (s)
  • F(\omega) — its Fourier transform, the signal in the frequency domain (called X(\omega) above): how much of each frequency the signal contains, as a complex number (size = amount, angle = phase)
  • \omega — angular frequency (rad/s)
  • i — the imaginary unit, i^2 = -1
  • e^{-i\omega t} = \cos(\omega t) - i\sin(\omega t) — a rotating "test wave" at frequency \omega; the integral measures how well the signal matches it
  • The second formula is the inverse transform: it rebuilds f(t) from its frequencies

(Figure: a square wave in the time domain built from sinusoids at 1/T, 3/T, 5/T, …, shown as spikes in the frequency domain.)

Intuition

The Fourier transform answers "how much of each frequency is in this signal?". e^{-i\omega t} is a rotating pointer at frequency \omega; multiplying the signal by it and integrating measures how strongly the signal "keeps pace" with that rotation — large if the signal contains that frequency, near zero if not. The inverse transform rebuilds the signal by adding all those sinusoids back up. Filtering is then simple to describe: in the frequency domain, multiply the unwanted frequencies by (nearly) zero.

Filter types

Low-pass: passes frequencies below the cut-off f_c, blocks above. High-pass: the opposite. The cut-off is where the response has dropped by 3 dB.

Band-pass: passes the band between f_1 and f_2 around f_0 (passband bandwidth), blocks both sides. Notch (band-stop): blocks a narrow band around f_0, passes everything else.

Worked example — which filter for which problem?
  1. Noisy distance sensor, the true distance changes slowly: the noise is fast, the signal slow → low-pass.
  2. Accelerometer on a vehicle, you want vibrations but not the constant gravity offset (DC): remove the lowest frequencies → high-pass.
  3. Mains hum at 50 Hz on a sensor cable: remove one narrow frequency → notch at 50 Hz.
  4. Ultrasonic receiver listening for its own 40 kHz echo: keep only the band around 40 kHz → band-pass.
Common mistake

Expecting a filter to separate signal from noise that share the same frequencies. A filter can only remove what is in a different frequency band. And every real filter costs something: a low-pass smooths but also delays the signal, which matters inside a control loop — a heavily filtered sensor makes a controller react late.

Path planning

Mission planning → motion planning (path planning, trajectory planning) → robot control (source: Faigl, 2020, Path Planning).

Real mobile robots

  • In a real deployment the problem is more complex:

    • the world is changing;
    • robots update their knowledge about the environment — localization, mapping and navigation;
    • new decisions have to be made based on feedback from the environment;
    • motion planning is part of the mission re-planning loop.
  • How to deal with real-world complexity? Relax constraints and consider realistic assumptions.

Motion planning / path planning notation

  • \mathcal{W} — the world model describes the robot's workspace; its boundary determines the obstacles \mathcal{O}.
  • A robot is defined by its geometry and parameters (kinematics) and is controllable by the motion plan.

  • Configuration space (C-space) — describes the possible configurations of the robot. A configuration completely specifies the robot's location in \mathcal{W}, including all degrees of freedom.

    • Collision-free configurations: \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{free}} = \mathcal{C} \setminus \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{O}}.
Symbols
  • \mathcal{C} — the configuration space: all configurations of the robot
  • \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{O}} — the configurations in which the robot collides with an obstacle from \mathcal{O}
  • \setminus — set difference: "everything in \mathcal{C} except what is in \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{O}}"
  • \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{free}} — the collision-free configurations
  • A path is a continuous mapping in C-space.

  • A trajectory is a path with an explicit parametrisation of time, e.g. accompanied by a description of the motion laws.

    • Additional requirements can be given: smoothness of the path; kinodynamic constraints (e.g. friction forces); an optimality criterion — shortest vs. fastest (length vs. curvature).
  • Path planning — planning a collision-free path in C-space.
  • Motion planning — planning collision-free motion in the state space.
Why plan in configuration space instead of the real workspace?

A real robot has a size and shape, so "is this position free?" depends on its whole body. In C-space the robot becomes a single point (one configuration = one point) and the obstacles are inflated accordingly; then "collision-free" simply means "the point stays in \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{free}}" and point-planning algorithms apply. For a round mobile robot this is easy to picture: grow every obstacle by the robot's radius and plan for a point — exactly the "grown obstacles" trick on the visibility-graph slide.

Graph theory

  • Graphs are data structures composed of nodes and edges.
  • Edges can carry weights (costs, e.g. distances) and can be directed.

Weighted graph with nodes A–F: A–B 3, A–C 9, A–D 1, B–C 4, B–E 3, C–F 2, D–F 3, E–F 1.

Worked example — shortest paths from A (Dijkstra's algorithm)

Idea: repeatedly settle the unsettled node with the smallest known distance, then update its neighbours.

  1. Start: d(A) = 0. Neighbours: B = 3, C = 9, D = 1.
  2. Settle D (1): via D, F = 1 + 3 = 4.
  3. Settle B (3): via B, E = 3 + 3 = 6, C = \min(9,\ 3 + 4) = 7.
  4. Settle F (4): via F, E = \min(6,\ 4 + 1) = 5, C = \min(7,\ 4 + 2) = 6.
  5. Settle E (5), then C (6). Done.
  6. Read off: A→C costs 6 via A–D–F–C — cheaper than the direct edge (9) or A–B–C (7). A→E costs 5 via A–D–F–E, beating A–B–E (6). The fewest edges is not the shortest path.

Path planning — visibility graph

  • The start, the goal and the vertices of the obstacles are graph nodes.
  • Edges are "visible" connections between nodes (straight lines that don't cross an obstacle), including the obstacle edges.
  • Search for the shortest path via the visible vertices.

Left: start, goal and polygonal obstacles. Right: the visibility graph (red) and the shortest path (yellow).

Reduced visibility graph:

  • The standard visibility graph has many needless edges that will never be used.
  • The useful lines go around the obstacles, or pass through the vertices that are extreme around the obstacles.
  • Eliminate unnecessary obstacle vertices: the shortest path doesn't change, and the time to find it decreases considerably.

Robot size:

  • The common visibility-graph algorithm assumes point robots.
  • It places waypoints on the obstacle boundaries, which increases the risk of collision.
  • Use C-space: expand each obstacle by the size of the robot (robot + obstacle = grown obstacle).
  • Graph search then finds the shortest path, if one exists, using the grown obstacle set.
Why does the shortest path always bend only at obstacle corners?

Picture a rubber band stretched from start to goal around the obstacles: it is straight wherever it is free, and it can only bend where something holds it — at a convex corner of an obstacle. Any bend in open space could be shortcut, making the path shorter. So the shortest path is a chain of straight segments between start, obstacle corners and goal — exactly the edges of the visibility graph, which is why searching that graph finds it.

Voronoi graph

  • The roadmap is the basis for the Voronoi graph, which maximises clearance from the obstacles.
  • The start and goal positions are connected to the graph.
  • The path is found with a graph search algorithm.

Voronoi graph of a cluttered map (lines equidistant from neighbouring obstacles), the path in the graph, and the found path.

Comparison

Visibility graphVoronoi graph
Pathshortest path, but close to obstacles — an error in plan execution can lead to a collision, so safety must be consideredmaximises clearance — conservative paths
Robustness—small changes in obstacles can lead to large changes in the graph
Dimensionscomplicated in higher dimensionscomplicated in higher dimensions

Visibility graph exercise

Start (0,0), goal (17,9). Two rectangular obstacles: the first with top-left corner (3,6) and bottom-right corner (7,2), the second with top-left (10,8) and bottom-right (16,4).

Worked example — solving the slide 44 exercise for a point robot
  1. Nodes: start, goal and the 8 corners: (3,2), (3,6), (7,2), (7,6) and (10,4), (10,8), (16,4), (16,8).

  2. Candidate routes (only via corners that "see" each other):

    • over both obstacles: (0,0) \to (3,6) \to (10,8) \to (17,9): \sqrt{45} + \sqrt{53} + \sqrt{50} \approx 6.71 + 7.28 + 7.07 = 21.06;
    • under both: (0,0) \to (16,4) \to (17,9) — the line y = x/4 passes below the first box: \sqrt{272} + \sqrt{26} \approx 16.49 + 5.10 = 21.59.
  3. Check visibility of the winner: (0,0)\to(3,6) touches box 1 only at its corner; (3,6)\to(10,8) passes above box 1's top edge (y = 6) and reaches box 2's corner; (10,8)\to(17,9) stays above box 2's top (y = 8).
  4. Answer: the shortest path goes over the obstacles via (3,6) and (10,8), length \approx 21.06 (checked with a full visibility-graph search). Note it grazes two corners — for a real robot, grow the boxes by its radius first.
Connection

The planner's output is the trajectory that the controllers of 6 Dynamics & Control follow and the inverse kinematics of 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics turn into joint angles. Graph search reappears in 10 Introduction to AI as a basic form of problem solving.
